callouts.title: Report Overview
callouts.body: This report provides a comprehensive foundational treatment of **Baddeley's Working Memory Model** — the dominant cognitive architecture of temporary, active information processing. Beginning from the model's intellectual origins in the failures of the unitary short-term memory construct, the report systematically treats each of the model's four components, examines its theoretical landscape and competing accounts, traces its mechanisms, and critically evaluates its applications, limitations, and open questions. The report concludes with an annotated expansion pathway for deeper investigation.

callouts.title: Why Working Memory Matters for Learning
callouts.body: Working memory is the **bottleneck of learning**. All new information must pass through working memory before it can be encoded into [[Long-Term-Memory]]. Its capacity constraints are not incidental — they are the fundamental constraint around which instructional design, knowledge organisation, and deliberate practice must be structured.

callouts.title: The Problem with Unitary Short-Term Memory
callouts.body: The [[Atkinson-Shiffrin-Multi-Store-Model]] (1968) proposed a three-stage architecture: sensory registers → a unitary short-term store (STS) → long-term memory. The STS was conceptualised as a single, passive holding buffer with rehearsal as its primary mechanism. **This model struggled to account for how people simultaneously store and process information** — a routine demand of virtually all cognitive tasks.

callouts.title: The Dual-Task Paradigm
callouts.body: Baddeley & Hitch's founding methodology was the **dual-task paradigm**: participants were required to maintain digit sequences in memory (loading the presumed short-term store) while simultaneously performing complex reasoning tasks. If the unitary STS was the primary working space for cognition, loading it should severely impair reasoning. The results were striking: **even with maximum digit-span loads, reasoning was slowed but not catastrophically impaired**. This suggested separate sub-systems — rehearsal and reasoning were drawing on different resources.

callouts.title: Working Memory (Baddeley, 2000)
callouts.body: **[[Working-Memory|Working memory]]** is "a brain system that provides temporary storage and manipulation of the information necessary for such complex cognitive tasks as language comprehension, learning, and reasoning." It is not merely passive storage but an *active processing workspace* with multiple specialised subsystems coordinated by a limited-capacity attentional controller.

callouts.title: The Central Executive
callouts.body: The [[Central-Executive]] is an **attentionally limited control system** responsible for coordinating the slave systems, directing attentional focus, switching between tasks, inhibiting irrelevant information, and activating long-term memory representations. It has no dedicated storage capacity of its own — it is a *processor*, not a *store*.

callouts.title: The Homunculus Problem
callouts.body: The central executive is theoretically vulnerable to a **homunculus regress**: explaining attention by positing an inner "executive" that itself requires explaining. Baddeley acknowledged this limitation explicitly and encouraged fractionation research to decompose the executive into specific, measurable sub-functions. Researchers like Randall Engle reframe the central executive as *executive attention* — the ability to maintain goal-relevant representations against interference — which is more tractable experimentally.

callouts.title: The Phonological Loop
callouts.body: The **[[Phonological-Loop]]** is a limited-capacity, time-based system comprising two sub-components: (1) a **phonological store** that holds speech-sound traces for approximately 1.5–2 seconds before they decay, and (2) an **articulatory rehearsal process** (the "inner voice") that refreshes decaying traces by sub-vocally re-encoding them in phonological form.

callouts.title: Word Length Effect
callouts.body: Immediate serial recall is better for lists of **short words** than long words — because short words can be rehearsed more rapidly, allowing more items to be refreshed within the ~2-second articulatory loop cycle. This temporal constraint, not syllabic complexity per se, is the operative mechanism (Baddeley, Thomson & Buchanan, 1975).

callouts.title: Phonological Similarity Effect
callouts.body: Sequences of phonologically similar items (e.g., *b, d, g, p, t*) are harder to recall in correct order than phonologically distinct items. Crucially, this effect persists even with visually presented letters — demonstrating that the phonological store encodes speech-based representations even when input is visual (Conrad & Hull, 1964).

callouts.title: Articulatory Suppression
callouts.body: Having participants repeat an irrelevant sound (e.g., "the, the, the...") during memorisation eliminates the word length effect for visually presented items and attenuates the phonological similarity effect. This suppression occupies the articulatory rehearsal mechanism, preventing sub-vocal recoding — **the clearest evidence that the articulatory rehearsal process, not merely the store, is critical for maintenance of phonological representations.**

callouts.title: The Visuospatial Sketchpad
callouts.body: The **[[Visuospatial-Sketchpad]]** is a limited-capacity system for maintaining and transforming visual and spatial representations — including mental images, spatial layouts, and object tracking. It is fractionated into: (1) a **visual cache** (the "what" system — object features, colour, shape) and (2) an **inner scribe** (the "where/how" system — spatial and movement information).

callouts.title: Practical Illustration: Navigation and Design
callouts.body: When a chess player plans several moves ahead, mentally rotating the board, they are loading the visuospatial sketchpad. When an architect mentally "walks through" a building design, or when a driver tracks the spatial positions of adjacent vehicles, the sketchpad bears the primary representational burden. Disruptions to this system (e.g., spatial tasks while driving) produce characteristic interference patterns predicted by the dual-resource account.

callouts.title: The Episodic Buffer
callouts.body: The **[[Episodic-Buffer]]** is a limited-capacity, temporary storage system that integrates information from the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and [[Long-Term-Memory]] into unified, multi-dimensional **episodes** — coherent, consciously accessible representations that bind features across domains and modalities.

callouts.title: Consciousness and the Episodic Buffer
callouts.body: Baddeley proposed that the episodic buffer interfaces with **conscious awareness** — it provides a "multimodal stage" on which a coherent conscious episode is constructed. This makes it relevant to theories of consciousness, though the specific mechanisms remain underspecified. The buffer is assumed to be read by the central executive but is not itself assumed to have executive functions.

callouts.title: Cowan's Capacity Estimate: ~4 Chunks
callouts.body: Using change-detection paradigms — where participants must detect whether a test display matches a memorised array — Cowan (2001) found robust evidence for a capacity limit of approximately **4 items** (chunks), substantially lower than Miller's 7 ± 2. This difference likely reflects that Miller's original paradigm allowed for rehearsal and chunking, while change-detection tasks better isolate the core limited-capacity focus of attention.

callouts.title: WM Capacity and Individual Differences
callouts.body: Working memory capacity measured by complex span tasks correlates with fluid intelligence at r ≈ .50–.70, reading comprehension, following complex instructions, controlled attention in dichotic listening, and resistance to proactive interference. High-capacity individuals show superior ability to maintain task-relevant goals against distraction; low-capacity individuals are more susceptible to mind-wandering and interference — a pattern consistent with the executive attention account.

callouts.title: The Expertise-WM Interaction
callouts.body: [[Expertise]] systematically alters how working memory operates: expert chess players, expert surgeons, and expert programmers effectively "offload" to [[Long-Term-Memory]] by employing richly organised schemas. What occupies multiple working memory slots for a novice occupies one slot for an expert — a principle with profound implications for [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] and [[Automaticity]].

callouts.title: Measuring Phonological Loop Capacity
callouts.body: **Word span** — the longest list of words that can be immediately recall perfectly on 50% of trials — is the standard phonological loop measure. **Digit span** is its most common application. Both are well-standardised and highly reliable. **Articulatory suppression** (concurrent irrelevant articulation) selectively disrupts the articulatory rehearsal component, providing a clean method to separate store from rehearsal contributions.

callouts.title: Mental Rotation as Sketchpad Work
callouts.body: Shepard & Metzler's (1971) landmark experiments showed that the time required to judge whether two 3D shapes are identical (one rotated relative to the other) increases linearly with the angle of rotation. This analogue, time-continuous relationship suggests that rotation is being performed mentally — the sketchpad is operating on a spatial representation, not merely comparing symbolic descriptions.

callouts.title: Decay Theory
callouts.body: Traces fade over time due to passive biological processes unless actively refreshed through rehearsal. Baddeley's phonological loop explicitly incorporates a decay account — the ~2 second time window reflects trace decay rate governing maintenance capacity.

callouts.title: Interference Theory
callouts.body: Forgetting is primarily caused by interference from other representations, not passive time-based decay. Computational models by Oberauer and others suggest that interference from proactive (earlier items) and retroactive (newer items) intrusions accounts for most working memory failures without requiring a decay mechanism.

callouts.title: CLT as Applied Working Memory Science
callouts.body: [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] is essentially the engineering application of Baddeley's model: it provides design principles for keeping extraneous load low (reducing wasteful processing), managing intrinsic load (sequencing, segmenting, worked examples), and optimising germane load (elaboration, variation, retrieval practice). Every major CLT effect — the worked example effect, the split-attention effect, the modality effect, the redundancy effect — can be traced to working memory architecture.

callouts.title: Clinical Relevance
callouts.body:
- **ADHD**: Core working memory deficits — especially in updating and inhibition — are among the most reliable cognitive markers of ADHD. These reflect central executive weaknesses, and explain inattention to task-relevant goals and susceptibility to distraction.
- **Normal ageing**: Working memory, particularly the central executive component, declines across the adult lifespan. Timothy Salthouse's processing speed account links this decline to reduced speed of attentional refreshing.
- **Specific Learning Disability / Dyslexia**: Phonological loop deficits are the most consistent cognitive profile associated with dyslexia, impairing phonological awareness and reading acquisition.
- **Schizophrenia**: Central executive and prefrontal working memory impairments are among the most replicated cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

callouts.title: Modality Effect in Instruction
callouts.body: Presenting verbal explanations as **spoken audio** (loading the phonological loop) while simultaneously presenting **diagrams** (loading the visuospatial sketchpad) exploits the dual-channel architecture. Both channels are occupied, but because they are separate, total capacity is effectively doubled compared to presenting verbal explanation as on-screen text alongside a diagram (which loads both phonological and visuospatial systems through visual processing). This is the **modality effect** in CLT and Mayer's Multimedia Learning.

callouts.title: The Model's Enduring Contributions
callouts.body:
1. **Empirical productivity**: The model has generated thousands of testable predictions and guided five decades of experimental research.
2. **Component dissociation**: Domain-specific impairments in patients (verbal vs. spatial memory) strongly validate the component architecture.
3. **Dual-task paradigm**: The experimental methodology has proven extraordinarily powerful and is now standard across cognitive science.
4. **Applied reach**: [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]], multimedia learning, neuropsychological assessment, educational psychology, and cognitive ageing research all derive principal organising constructs from Baddeley's framework.

callouts.title: Limitations That Remain Unresolved
callouts.body:
1. **The central executive as homunculus**: Despite efforts at fractionation, the central executive still risks circularity — the "executive" has not been fully replaced by mechanistic accounts of its constituent functions.
2. **The episodic buffer's underspecification**: How exactly does the buffer bind information? What is the mechanism of conscious access? The 2000 proposal opened important questions without fully closing them.
3. **The WM/LTM boundary problem**: Whether working memory is a functionally distinct system or merely activated long-term memory remains contested. Long-Term Working Memory (Ericsson & Kintsch, 1995) and the Embedded Processes account challenge the strict separability assumption.
4. **Capacity measurement variability**: Estimates ranging from 4 to 7 items reflect different tasks measuring different things — the construct is not yet measured with the precision the theory assumes.
5. **Neural basis ambiguity**: While prefrontal and parietal regions are consistently activated, they are not cleanly separable by component — the one-to-one mapping between cognitive components and brain regions has not been established.

callouts.title: Unresolved Frontier Questions
callouts.body:
- **What is the unit of working memory capacity** — items, chunks, features, activation strength? The right unit of measurement shapes theoretically very different architectures.
- **Is there really a phonological loop in reading**, or does reading bypass it? The evidence is mixed for skilled adult readers.
- **Can working memory capacity be trained** — and if so, what transfers? The commercial "brain training" literature has failed to show transfer beyond trained tasks; the theoretical explanation implicates the executive attention account (capacity limits reflect fixed structural constraints, not trainable content).
- **How does the episodic buffer interface with conscious experience** — is it the "global workspace" posited by Baars, or distinct from it?
- **How does sleep modulate working memory** — is consolidation from working memory to long-term memory possible without a hippocampal interface mediated by sleep?

callouts.title: What the Baddeley Model Achieves
callouts.body: Baddeley's Working Memory Model achieves something rare in cognitive science: **a sufficiently specified, multi-component architecture that is both empirically tractable and theoretically productive**. Its four components map coherently onto neural evidence, clinical profiles, developmental trajectories, and instructional phenomena. Its limitations — the homunculus risk in the central executive, the underspecified episodic buffer — are not fatal flaws but research boundaries that have generated, and continue to generate, productive inquiry.

callouts.title: Core Takeaways
callouts.body:
1. Working memory is **multi-component**, not unitary — storage and processing draw on separable subsystems.
2. The **phonological loop** is time-based, speech-coded, and critical for language and early literacy.
3. The **visuospatial sketchpad** is dual-natured (visual + spatial) and supports imagery, navigation, and geometric reasoning.
4. The **central executive** is the attentional controller — its capacity is the primary limiting factor in complex cognition.
5. The **episodic buffer** integrates across modalities and interfaces with long-term episodic memory.
6. Working memory capacity (~4 chunks of attention) is the **primary architectural constraint** around which all learning design must be oriented.
7. [[Expertise]] and [[Automaticity]] systematically reduce working memory load by offloading to [[Long-Term-Memory]] schemas.

wiki_links.section: Phase I: Orientation & Context Setting
wiki_links.context_line: Working memory occupies the conceptual centre of cognitive psychology. It is the cognitive workspace — the system by which the mind actively holds and manipulates information over seconds, bridging perception, knowledge retrieval, and goal-directed behaviour. Understanding its architecture is foundational to understanding [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]], [[Learning-Science]], instructional design, reading, mathematical reasoning, language acquisition, and clinical assessment of [[Executive-Function]] disorders.

wiki_links.context_line: [[George-Miller]]'s landmark 1956 paper, introducing the concept of the "[[Miller's-Magical-Number-Seven|magical number seven plus or minus two]]," established empirically that short-term memory capacity is severely limited — roughly 7 ± 2 items, or more precisely, 7 ± 2 *chunks* of meaningfully organised information. wiki_links.section: The Intellectual Genealogy: From Storage to Processing
wiki_links.context_line: The crucial observation that motivated Baddeley and Hitch came from neuropsychological evidence and dual-task experiments. Patients with severely impaired short-term memory (e.g., patient KF, studied by Warrington & Shallice) showed largely intact [[Long-Term-Memory]] acquisition, contradicting the Atkinson-Shiffrin claim that the STS was the obligatory gateway to long-term learning. The STS-as-bottleneck model was empirically untenable.

wiki_links.section: Component 1: The Central Executive
wiki_links.context_line: The [[Central-Executive]] is the supervisory attentional system of working memory — the most powerful and least understood component. Baddeley explicitly modelled it on the **Supervisory Attentional System (SAS)** proposed by Norman and Shallice (1986), which distinguishes between routine, schema-driven behaviour and attention-demanding, controlled action.

wiki_links.section: Component 1: The Central Executive
wiki_links.context_line: The central executive is heavily implicated in [[Executive-Function]] more broadly — the set of higher-order regulatory processes including planning, cognitive flexibility, and inhibitory control. wiki_links.context_line: The [[Phonological-Loop]] is the best-understood component of working memory — the "inner voice and inner ear" system specialised for phonological (speech-sound) information.

wiki_links.section: Component 2: The Phonological Loop
wiki_links.context_line: [**Articulatory-Rehearsal**:: The active sub-vocal repetition process of the phonological loop's [[Articulatory-Construction-Principle|articulatory rehearsal mechanism]] — the "inner voice" — that refreshes decaying traces in the phonological store, enabling maintenance beyond the ~2 second natural decay window.]

wiki_links.section: Component 2: The Phonological Loop
wiki_links.context_line: **Developmental significance:** The phonological loop plays a critical role in [[Working-Memory-in-Reading|reading acquisition]] and vocabulary learning in children. Susan Gathercole's extensive research shows that phonological loop capacity predicts early reading skill and vocabulary acquisition — the loop serves as a temporary phonological holding space during the process of learning new word forms. Children with specific language impairment typically show marked phonological loop deficits.

wiki_links.context_line: The [[Visuospatial-Sketchpad]] is the "inner eye" — the component dedicated to the temporary storage and manipulation of visual and spatial information.

It is fractionated into: (1) a **visual cache** (the "what" system — object features, colour, shape) and (2) an **inner scribe** (the "where/how" system — spatial and movement information).

wiki_links.section: Component 3: The Visuospatial Sketchpad
wiki_links.context_line: [**Dual-Resource-Account**:: The principle, derived from the sketchpad's visual/spatial fractionation, that concurrent tasks sharing the same sub-resource (e.g., two spatial tasks) produce greater mutual interference than tasks drawing on different sub-resources — with major implications for multi-modal instructional design and [[Dual-Coding-Theory]].]

wiki_links.section: Cowan's Embedded Processes Model
wiki_links.context_line: Nelson Cowan's [[Working-Memory|Embedded Processes Model]] (1988, 1995, 2001) offers the most influential alternative framing. Where Baddeley posits distinct dedicated components, Cowan argues that working memory is not a separate system but rather the currently activated portion of long-term memory, with a focus of attention (~3–4 chunks) at its centre.

wiki_links.section: Engle's Executive Attention Account
wiki_links.context_line: Randall Engle and colleagues' research programme reconceptualises [[Working-Memory-Capacity|working memory capacity]] as primarily a measure of **executive attention** — the ability to actively maintain goal-relevant representations in the face of interference and distraction. Complex working memory span tasks (reading span, operation span) predict fluid intelligence, academic achievement, and susceptibility to executive failures precisely because they measure this controlled, interference-resistant maintenance capacity.

wiki_links.section: The Relationship Between Working Memory and Long-Term Memory
wiki_links.context_line: A fundamental theoretical tension concerns whether working memory and [[Long-Term-Memory]] are separate systems or whether working memory is simply activated long-term memory. [[Schema-Theory-and-Learning|Schema theory]] and [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] offer directly relevant perspectives: as expertise develops, complex schemas in [[Long-Term-Memory]] can be treated as single chunks in working memory, dramatically reducing effective load.

wiki_links.section: The Relationship Between Working Memory and Long-Term Memory
wiki_links.context_line: A fundamental theoretical tension concerns whether working memory and [[Long-Term-Memory]] are separate systems or whether working memory is simply activated long-term memory. [[Schema-Theory-and-Learning|Schema theory]] and [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] offer directly relevant perspectives: as expertise develops, complex schemas in [[Long-Term-Memory]] can be treated as single chunks in working memory, dramatically reducing effective load.

wiki_links.section: The Relationship Between Working Memory and Long-Term Memory
wiki_links.context_line: > [[Expertise]] systematically alters how working memory operates: expert chess players, expert surgeons, and expert programmers effectively "offload" to [[Long-Term-Memory]] by employing richly organised schemas. What occupies multiple working memory slots for a novice occupies one slot for an expert — a principle with profound implications for [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] and [[Automaticity]].

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: The most educationally consequential application of Baddeley's model is [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] (Sweller, 1988), which operationalises the working memory bottleneck for instructional design. The three-load framework maps directly:

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: - **[[Intrinsic-Cognitive-Load]]**: The inherent complexity of the material — determined by the number of interacting elements that must be held simultaneously in working memory

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: - **[[Extraneous-Cognitive-Load]]**: Unnecessary working memory demand created by poor instructional design — formats that require searching, splitting attention, or redundant processing

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: - **[[Germane-Cognitive-Load]]**: Effort devoted to schema construction and [[Long-Term-Memory]] integration — what the working memory is doing when it is being *useful* for learning

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: - **[[Germane-Cognitive-Load]]**: Effort devoted to schema construction and [[Long-Term-Memory]] integration — what the working memory is doing when it is being *useful* for learning

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: > [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] is essentially the engineering application of Baddeley's model: it provides design principles for keeping extraneous load low (reducing wasteful processing), managing intrinsic load (sequencing, segmenting, worked examples), and optimising germane load (elaboration, variation, retrieval practice). Every major CLT effect — the worked example effect, the split-attention effect, the modality effect, the redundancy effect — can be traced to working memory architecture.

wiki_links.section: Working Memory and Cognitive Load Theory
wiki_links.context_line: [**CLT-WM-Link**:: Cognitive Load Theory's three-load framework (intrinsic, extraneous, germane) directly operationalises working memory architecture — intrinsic load reflects element interactivity demanding simultaneous WM retention; extraneous load arises from avoidable WM competition; germane load is WM deployed for schema construction in [[Long-Term-Memory]].]

wiki_links.section: Working Memory in Reading and Language
wiki_links.context_line: [[Working-Memory-in-Reading|Reading comprehension]] depends heavily on the phonological loop for maintaining sentence-level phonological representations during parsing, and on the central executive for integrating information across clauses and paragraphs into a coherent [[Mental-Model]]. Poor readers consistently show lower phonological loop capacity; poor text comprehensors show lower central executive capacity even with intact decoding.

inline_fields.value: This report focuses specifically on the Baddeley multi-component model of working memory (1974, 2000), distinguishing it from broader memory systems treatments and from the competing Embedded Processes account of Cowan (2001).

The Atkinson-Shiffrin Multi-Store Model (1968) treated the short-term store as unitary and passive, limiting its explanatory power for active cognitive processing — the primary limitation that motivated Baddeley & Hitch's reconceptualisation.

The experimental method of concurrently loading short-term storage while requiring complex cognitive processing, used by Baddeley & Hitch (1974) to demonstrate that storage and processing draw on separable cognitive resources — the founding empirical strategy of working memory research.

The supervisory attentional system of working memory that directs and coordinates the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad, manages attentional focus, supports task-switching, and enables inhibitory control — modelled on Norman & Shallice's Supervisory Attentional System.

The working memory function of monitoring and replacing the contents of active working memory representations as incoming information supersedes prior content — a core component of fluid task performance.

Engle's reframing of working memory capacity as the ability to maintain goal-relevant representations in the face of interference and distraction — empirically operationalised through complex span tasks and correlates strongly with measures of fluid intelligence.

The passive acoustic-phonological trace store of the phonological loop, which holds speech-based memory representations for approximately 1.5–2 seconds before decay — equivalent to the "inner ear" in Baddeley's original metaphor.
The active sub-vocal repetition process of the phonological loop's [[Articulatory-Construction-Principle|articulatory rehearsal mechanism

The phonological loop functions as a critical substrate for vocabulary acquisition and reading development in children — by holding novel phonological word-forms while they are being mapped to orthographic representations and semantic meaning, a mechanism evidenced by Gathercole & Baddeley's developmental research programme.

The static visual component of the visuospatial sketchpad that holds object feature information such as colour, shape, and orientation — dissociable from the spatial rehearsal component (inner scribe) both cognitively and neurologically.

The spatial and movement sub-component of the visuospatial sketchpad responsible for rehearsing and refreshing spatial information through a spatial rehearsal loop — disrupted by concurrent spatial tracking tasks (e.g., arm movements in darkness).

The principle, derived from the sketchpad's visual/spatial fractionation, that concurrent tasks sharing the same sub-resource (e.g., two spatial tasks) produce greater mutual interference than tasks drawing on different sub-resources — with major implications for multi-modal instructional design and [[Dual-Coding-Theory

A fourth working memory component (Baddeley, 2000) that serves as a multi-modal integration workspace binding phonological, visuospatial, and long-term memory-sourced information into coherent episodic representations — accessible to conscious awareness and serving as the interface between working memory and long-term episodic memory.
The capacity of the [[Episodic-Buffer

Nelson Cowan's ~4 chunk estimate of the core attentional focus of working memory, derived from change-detection paradigms that minimise rehearsal and chunking, challenging Miller's higher 7±2 estimate and providing a converging estimate with the episodic buffer's proposed capacity.

Complex span tasks (e.g., reading span, operation span, counting span) that interleave to-be-remembered items with processing demands — they measure the capacity to maintain memory representations under concurrent processing load, operationalising the executive attention component of working memory.
The progressive transfer of working memory load to [[Long-Term-Memory

The central debate in the mechanistic account of working memory forgetting: whether traces are lost through passive time-based decay (Baddeley's position for the phonological loop) or through interference from competing representations (Oberauer, Lewandowsky, and the computational modelling tradition).

A maintenance mechanism distinct from articulatory rehearsal, in which the central executive briefly directs attention to a working memory representation to strengthen it — available for both verbal and non-verbal content and consumed by competing attention demands.

Cognitive Load Theory's three-load framework (intrinsic, extraneous, germane) directly operationalises working memory architecture — intrinsic load reflects element interactivity demanding simultaneous WM retention; extraneous load arises from avoidable WM competition; germane load is WM deployed for schema construction in [[Long-Term-Memory

The unresolved theoretical question of whether working memory constitutes a fundamentally distinct cognitive system or is better understood as the temporary activation of long-term memory representations — with Long-Term Working Memory (Ericsson & Kintsch) and the Embedded Processes model (Cowan) offering alternative frameworks that blur this boundary.

Baddeley's multi-component model represents a rare convergence of empirical tractability (component-specific experimental dissociations), neural plausibility (prefrontal and parietal working memory networks), developmental validity (phonological loop in language acquisition), and applied productivity (Cognitive Load Theory, multimedia learning, clinical assessment).

A limited-capacity cognitive system for the temporary, active storage and manipulation of information required for complex cognitive tasks — comprising the central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; Baddeley, 2000).
The passive, time-limited (approximately 2 seconds) trace store for phonological (speech-sound) representations — one sub-component of the phonological loop, subject to decay without rehearsal.

The inner voice mechanism of the phonological loop that refreshes decaying phonological traces by sub-vocalising them — blocked by articulatory suppression tasks and responsible for the word length effect.

The working memory component responsible for storing and manipulating visual and spatial representations — fractionated into a visual cache (features, objects) and an inner scribe (spatial/movement information).

The attentionally limited cognitive controller of working memory — coordinates slave systems, allocates attention, enables task switching and inhibitory control; modelled on the Norman-Shallice Supervisory Attentional System; theoretically the most powerful and least understood component.
A limited-capacity, multi-modal integration workspace added to Baddeley's model in 2000 — binds phonological, visuospatial, and [[Long-Term-Memory

The finding that immediate serial recall is better for short words than long words, attributed to the temporal constraint of the articulatory rehearsal loop — words that take longer to articulate require more time to rehearse, reducing the number that can be maintained within the ~2 second decay window.

The finding that sequences of phonologically similar items (sharing many speech sounds) are harder to recall in correct serial order than phonologically distinct items — demonstrating that the phonological store codes information in phonological, not semantic or orthographic, format.

The experimental technique of requiring participants to repeatedly utter an irrelevant word or sound during memorisation — occupies the articulatory rehearsal mechanism and selectively disrupts the phonological loop's rehearsal-based maintenance, abolishing the word length effect.

An experimental method used extensively by Cowan and others to estimate working memory capacity by presenting arrays of objects and testing whether participants can detect a change in one item — yields ~4 chunk capacity estimates by minimising rehearsal and chunking opportunities.

the currently activated portion of long-term memory

ordered.text: **Attentional focusing and dividing** — directing limited attention selectively or across multiple streams
**Task switching** — shifting between tasks or mental sets without catastrophic interference
**Inhibition** — suppressing irrelevant or prepotent responses to maintain goal-relevance
**Updating** — monitoring and refreshing the contents of working memory as task demands change
**Retrieval from long-term memory** — activating relevant knowledge to inform current processing

**The binding problem**: How do colour, shape, location, and phonological label of an object become integrated into a single unified representation? The phonological loop and sketchpad operate in separate coding formats with no clear mechanism for cross-modal binding.

**Chunking from LTM**: Why can people immediately recall 15-word sentences (far beyond ~4-7 slot capacity) if they are meaningful? LTM knowledge enables chunking, but the original model had no component to hold these LTM-enriched, bound episodes.
**Prose recall**: Immediate memory for connected text exceeds predictions from either slave system alone — something integrates verbal and contextual information coherently.

unordered.text: A **[[Central-Executive]]** — an attentionally limited control system
A **phonological loop** — a speech-based, time-limited storage and rehearsal system
A **visuospatial sketchpad** — a system for maintaining and manipulating visual and spatial information

**Brooks's dual-task studies**: Recalling a spatial sequence while making spatial movements (e.g., tracking a path) is more disrupted than visual-verbal combinations — demonstrating the modality-specific demand of the spatial sub-system.
**Corsi Block Test**: Spatial span (reproducing sequences of block taps) is largely dissociable from verbal span — providing direct capacity measurement of the visuospatial component.

**Mental rotation tasks**: Performance on mental rotation (Shepard & Metzler, 1971) draws on the visuospatial sketchpad — rotation time is proportional to angular disparity, consistent with an analogue spatial representation.

**Neuroimaging**: Visuospatial working memory activates parietal regions (especially posterior parietal cortex and the right hemisphere dorsal pathway), distinct from the left-lateralised frontoparietal network for verbal working memory.
Operates independently of the phonological loop (it can maintain visual and spatial information)
Is controlled by the central executive
Is limited by the rate at which attention can cycle across items
Is disrupted by attention-demanding tasks even when explicit rehearsal is blocked
**[[Intrinsic-Cognitive-Load]]**: The inherent complexity of the material — determined by the number of interacting elements that must be held simultaneously in working memory
**[[Extraneous-Cognitive-Load]]**: Unnecessary working memory demand created by poor instructional design — formats that require searching, splitting attention, or redundant processing
**[[Germane-Cognitive-Load]]**: Effort devoted to schema construction and [[Long-Term-Memory]] integration — what the working memory is doing when it is being *useful* for learning

**Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974)**. Working memory. In G. Bower (Ed.), *The psychology of learning and motivation* (Vol. 8). The founding paper — establishes the tripartite architecture through systematic dual-task experimentation.
**Baddeley, A. D. (2000)**. The episodic buffer: A new component of working memory? *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*. Introduces the fourth component, addressing binding and LTM interface limitations.
**Baddeley, A. D. (2007)**. *Working Memory, Thought, and Action*. Oxford University Press. The definitive authoritative treatment by the model's primary architect.

**Cowan, N. (2001)**. The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*. Landmark re-evaluation of capacity estimates with extensive peer commentary.

**Engle, R. W., Tuholski, S. W., Laughlin, J. E., & Conway, A. R. A. (1999)**. Working memory, short-term memory, and general fluid intelligence. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*. Key paper establishing WM capacity as executive attention and its relationship to fluid intelligence.
**Miller, G. A. (1956)**. The magical number seven, plus or minus two. *Psychological Review*. Pre-Baddeley classic establishing capacity limits and [[Chunking]].
**Sweller, J. (1988)**. Cognitive load during problem solving. *Cognitive Science*. The seminal application of working memory architecture to instructional design, founding [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]].
**Gathercole, S. E., & Baddeley, A. D. (1993)**. *Working Memory and Language*. Psychology Press. Comprehensive treatment of phonological loop's role in language and development.
*Connection*: CLT is the direct instructional-design application of working memory capacity limits — intrinsic, extraneous, and germane loads map precisely onto Baddeley's architecture
*Depth Potential*: Full treatment of CLT's design principles (worked examples, split-attention, modality, redundancy effects) builds on this report as foundational prerequisite
*Knowledge Graph Role*: Primary downstream node — the most applied and educationally consequential consequence of working memory science

*Connection*: The central executive is an attentional control system — a full treatment of selective attention, executive attention, and interference control deepens understanding of working memory's control architecture
*Depth Potential*: Treisman's Feature Integration Theory, Engle's executive attention programme, and Posner's attention networks all provide mechanistic scaffolding for the central executive
*Knowledge Graph Role*: Upstream conceptual node — attention theory provides the theoretical foundation for the central executive's function

*Connection*: Individual differences in WM capacity are among the strongest predictors of fluid intelligence, reading comprehension, and learning outcomes — the focused analysis examines measurement, heritability, and training evidence
*Depth Potential*: Complex span tasks, the n-back debate, heritability estimates, and the failure of working memory training to produce transfer
*Knowledge Graph Role*: Narrowing specification node — this report covers the architecture; WM capacity focuses on individual differences and measurement

*Connection*: Craik & Lockhart's (1972) levels of processing framework challenged the structural model by emphasising processing *quality* (depth of elaboration) over storage capacity — the relationship between encoding depth and working memory processes remains theoretically important
*Depth Potential*: Elaboration, distinctiveness, and transfer-appropriate processing as encoding principles that complement the architectural account
*Knowledge Graph Role*: Sibling theoretical node — provides a processing-quality account that complements Baddeley's structural-architectural account of the same cognitive territory
